title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: Sometimes, thinking over these matters alone, I rose in sudden terror and put on my bonnet to go and see how things stood at the farm. I persuaded my conscience that I ought to warn him what people were saying about his behaviour. Then I remembered how firmly his bad habits held him, and, despairing of doing him any good, shrank from entering that gloomy house again, unsure I could bear the fulfilment of my own warnings.

Once, on my way to Gimmerton, I made a detour past the old gate. It was about the time my story has now reached, a bright, frosty afternoon, with bare ground and a dry, hard road. I came to the stone where the road branches left onto the moor: a rough sandstone pillar with W. H. cut into its northern side, G. on the east and T. G. on the southwest, pointing to the Heights, the village and the Grange. Yellow sunlight on its grey top reminded me of summer, and I cannot explain why, but suddenly my heart flooded with the feelings of childhood. Hindley and I had loved that spot twenty years earlier. I stared for a long time at the weathered stone, then bent down and saw a hole near its base still full of snail shells and pebbles, which we used to store there with things that did not last so well. As vividly as in real life, I seemed to see my childhood playmate on the withered grass, his dark, square head bent, his small hand scraping earth out with a piece of slate. “Poor Hindley!” I exclaimed without meaning to. I started: for a moment my actual eyes were deceived into seeing the child lift his face and look straight into mine! He vanished instantly, but I felt an irresistible longing to reach the Heights. Superstition urged me to follow it: suppose he was dead! I thought—or soon to die! Suppose this was a death warning! The nearer I came, the more agitated I grew; when the house appeared I shook in every limb. The apparition had got there first and stood peering through the gate. That was my first thought on seeing a brown-eyed boy with tangled hair press his rosy face against the bars. A moment's reflection told me it must be Hareton, _my_ Hareton, little changed from the child I had left ten months before.
“God bless thee, darling!” I cried, forgetting my foolish fears at once. “Hareton, it's Nelly! Thy nurse, Nelly.”
He moved beyond my reach and picked up a big flint.
“I've come to see thy father, Hareton,” I added, guessing from this action that, if he remembered Nelly at all, he did not recognise her in me.

He lifted the stone to throw it. I began speaking soothingly but could not stop his hand: it struck my bonnet. Then a string of curses came stumbling from the little boy's lips, delivered with practised force whether or not he understood them, twisting his baby face into a shocking look of malice. You may be sure I felt more hurt than angry. Almost crying, I took an orange from my pocket and offered it to win him over. After hesitating he snatched it from me, as though he thought I only meant to tempt him and refuse it. I produced another, holding it beyond his reach.
“Who taught you such fine language, my little bairn?” I asked. “Was it the curate?”
“Damn t' curate and thee! Give me that,” he answered.
“Tell me where you learned it and you can have it,” I said. “Who's teaching you?”
“Devil daddy,” he answered.
“And what lessons does daddy give you?” I went on.
He jumped for the orange and I lifted it higher. “What does he teach you?” I repeated.
“Nowt,” he said, “except to keep out of his way. Daddy can't stand me because I swear at him.”
“Ah! And the devil teaches you to swear at your father?” I remarked.
“Aye—no,” he said slowly.
“Then who does?”
“Heathcliff.”
I asked whether he was fond of Mr. Heathcliff.
“Aye!” he replied again.
When I tried to discover why, all I could get was, “I don't know. He pays dad back for what he gives me—he swears at daddy for swearing at me. Says I must do as I like.”
“So the curate isn't giving you lessons in reading and writing?” I asked next.
“No. They said t' curate would have his —— teeth knocked down his —— throat if he crossed t' doorstep. Heathcliff promised that!”

I gave him the orange and told him to inform his father that a woman named Nelly Dean was waiting by the garden gate to speak to him. He went up the path and inside, but Heathcliff, not Hindley, appeared on the doorstep. I immediately turned and ran down the road as fast as I could, not stopping until I reached the signpost, frightened as though I had summoned a goblin. This has little to do with Miss Isabella's affair, except that it strengthened my resolve to keep a close watch and do everything possible to prevent such corruption spreading to the Grange, even if thwarting Mrs. Linton's pleasure brought on a household storm.

When Heathcliff next visited, my young lady happened to be feeding pigeons in the courtyard. For three days she had not spoken to her sister-in-law, but she had also stopped her fretful complaints, which was a great relief. I knew Heathcliff never wasted an unnecessary courtesy on Miss Linton. Now, as soon as he saw her, he first carefully surveyed the entire front of the house. I stood at the kitchen window but stepped out of sight. He crossed the paving stones and spoke to her. She looked embarrassed and anxious to leave, so he put a hand on her arm to stop her. She turned her face away; apparently he asked something she did not want to answer. After another quick glance at the house, believing himself unseen, the scoundrel had the audacity to embrace her.
“Judas! Traitor!” I burst out. “So you're a hypocrite as well? A deliberate cheat.”
“Who is, Nelly?” Catherine asked beside me. I had watched the pair outside too intently to notice her arrival.

“That worthless friend of yours!” I replied hotly. “That sneaking rogue out there. Ah, he's seen us—he's coming inside! I wonder if he'll dare find a plausible excuse for courting Miss after telling you he hated her?”

Mrs. Linton saw Isabella break free and run into the garden. A minute later Heathcliff opened the door. I could not help giving vent to some of my outrage, but Catherine angrily ordered me to be quiet, threatening to send me out of the kitchen if I dared presume to put in my insolent opinions.

“Anyone hearing you would think you were the mistress!” she cried. “You need putting in your proper place! Heathcliff, what do you mean by causing this disturbance? I told you to leave Isabella alone! Please do, unless you're tired of being welcomed here and want Linton to lock you out!”
“God help him if he tries!” answered the dark villain—I hated him at that moment. “God keep him gentle and patient! Every day I'm more desperate to send him to heaven!”
“Hush!” Catherine said, closing the inner door. “Don't upset me. Why did you ignore my request? Did she deliberately put herself in your way?”
“What's that to you?” he growled. “I've a right to kiss her if she wants me to, and you've no right to complain. I'm not _your_ husband; _you_ have no reason to be jealous of me!”

“I'm not jealous of you,” the mistress replied. “I'm jealous on your behalf. Stop looking like that: you won't scowl at me! If you love Isabella, you shall marry her. But do you love her? Tell me honestly, Heathcliff! There, you won't answer. I'm sure you don't.”
“Would Mr. Linton agree to his sister marrying such a man?” I asked.
“Mr. Linton would have to agree,” my mistress answered firmly.

“He could save himself the trouble,” Heathcliff said. “I'd manage perfectly well without his approval. As for you, Catherine, while we're on the subject there's something I want to say. Understand that I _know_ you've treated me hellishly—hellishly! Do you hear? If you flatter yourself that I haven't noticed, you're a fool. If you think sweet words can console me, you're an idiot; and if you imagine I'll suffer without revenge, I'll soon show you otherwise! Meanwhile, thank you for revealing your sister-in-law's secret. I swear I'll make the most of it. And you keep out of the way!”

“What new side to his character is this?” Mrs. Linton exclaimed in amazement. “I've treated you hellishly, and you'll have revenge! How will you take it, you ungrateful brute? What have I done to you that's hellish?”

“I don't want revenge on you,” Heathcliff answered more quietly. “That isn't my plan. A tyrant grinds down his slaves, and instead of attacking him, they crush the people beneath them. You're welcome to torture me to death for your amusement: just let me amuse myself a little in the same way, and avoid insulting me as much as you can. After demolishing my palace, don't put up a hut and congratulate yourself on your kindness in giving me a home. If I believed you truly wanted me to marry Isabel, I'd cut my throat!”

“Oh, the trouble is that I'm _not_ jealous, is it?” Catherine exclaimed. “Well, I won't offer you a wife again. It's like offering Satan a lost soul: your happiness, like his, lies in causing misery, and you're proving it. Edgar has recovered from the bad temper your arrival put him in; I'm beginning to feel safe and peaceful. You can't bear to know we're at peace, and seem determined to stir up a quarrel. Quarrel with Edgar if you like, Heathcliff, and deceive his sister: that will be exactly the most effective revenge you can take on me.”

The conversation stopped. Mrs. Linton sat down beside the fire, flushed and gloomy. The spirit she had enlisted was becoming unmanageable: she could neither dismiss nor control it. He stood on the hearth, arms folded, brooding over his evil thoughts. I left them like this to find the master, who was wondering why Catherine remained downstairs so long.
“Ellen,” he asked when I came in, “have you seen where your mistress is?”

“Yes, sir, she's in the kitchen,” I replied. “Mr. Heathcliff's behaviour has upset her terribly. I really think the conditions of his visits need changing. Being too lenient does harm, and now matters have reached this point—” I described the scene outside and, as fully as I dared, the argument afterwards. I thought it could do Mrs. Linton little damage unless she chose to make it worse by defending her guest. Edgar Linton could hardly wait for me to finish. His first words showed that he did not consider his wife blameless.

“This is unbearable!” he exclaimed. “It's disgraceful that she calls him a friend and forces his company on me! Fetch two men from the hall, Ellen. Catherine won't stay down there arguing with that low ruffian any longer. I've indulged her quite enough.”

He went downstairs, told the servants to wait in the passage, and entered the kitchen with me behind him. The occupants had resumed their angry discussion; at least Mrs. Linton was scolding with fresh energy. Heathcliff had gone to the window and stood with his head lowered, apparently somewhat subdued by her fierce rebukes. He saw the master first and quickly signalled her to stop. Once she saw why, she fell abruptly silent.

“What is the meaning of this?” Linton asked her. “What sense of decency can you have, staying here after the way that scoundrel has spoken to you? I suppose it means nothing to you because that's how he always speaks. You're accustomed to his vileness, and perhaps expect me to become accustomed to it too!”

“Have you been eavesdropping, Edgar?” the mistress asked, in a voice peculiarly suited to provoking her husband, suggesting both indifference and contempt for his anger. Heathcliff had looked up during Edgar's speech; at Catherine's question he laughed scornfully, apparently intending to draw Mr. Linton's attention. He succeeded, but Edgar had no intention of entertaining him with extravagant anger.

“Until now, sir, I've treated you with patience,” he said quietly. “Not because I failed to understand your miserable, degraded character, but because I thought you only partly responsible for it. Catherine wished to maintain your acquaintance, and I foolishly agreed. Your presence is a moral poison that could corrupt the most virtuous person. For that reason, and to avoid worse consequences, I forbid you to enter this house again and now require you to leave immediately. If you delay three minutes, your departure will be forced and disgraceful.”
With a contemptuous eye, Heathcliff measured both the speaker's height and his breadth.
“Cathy, your lamb is making threats like a bull!” he said. “It risks cracking its skull against my fists. By God! Mr. Linton, I'm terribly sorry you aren't worth knocking down!”

My master glanced towards the passage and signalled for me to summon the men; he meant to risk no personal fight. I obeyed, but Mrs. Linton, suspecting something, followed me. As I tried to call them, she pulled me back, slammed the door and locked it.

“Fair play!” she said in answer to her husband's angry, astonished look. “If you aren't brave enough to attack him yourself, apologise or submit to a beating. That'll cure you of pretending to more courage than you have. No, I'll swallow the key before I give it up! What a lovely reward for my kindness to both of you! After endlessly indulging one man's weakness and the other's bad nature, my thanks are two examples of blind ingratitude, ridiculously stupid! Edgar, I was defending you and your family, and I hope Heathcliff beats you sick for daring to think ill of me!”

The master needed no beating to make him sick. He tried to wrest the key from Catherine's hand, and she threw it into the hottest part of the fire for safety. Mr. Edgar began trembling nervously and turned deathly pale. Nothing he could do prevented that overwhelming emotion: anguish and humiliation together defeated him completely. He leaned against the back of a chair and covered his face.

“Oh, heavens! In former days this would have earned you a knighthood!” Mrs. Linton exclaimed. “We're defeated! We're defeated! Heathcliff is no more likely to raise a finger against you than the king to send his army against a colony of mice. Cheer up! You won't be hurt! You're not a lamb, you're a little hare still at its mother's milk.”

“I wish you happiness with your milk-blooded coward, Cathy!” her friend said. “My compliments on your taste. And this drooling, trembling thing is what you preferred to me! I wouldn't strike him with my fist, but I'd kick him with my foot and enjoy it considerably. Is he crying, or about to faint from fright?”

The fellow stepped closer and shoved the chair Linton leaned on. He would have done better to keep his distance: my master sprang upright and struck him squarely in the throat, a blow that would have felled a less strongly built man. It left him breathless for a minute. While he choked, Mr. Linton walked through the back door into the yard and round to the front entrance.

“There! That's the end of your visits,” Catherine cried. “Go now: he'll be back with two pistols and half a dozen men. If he heard what we said, of course he'll never forgive you. You've done me an ill turn, Heathcliff! But leave—hurry! I'd rather see Edgar cornered than you.”

“Do you think I'm leaving with that blow burning in my throat?” he thundered. “By hell, no! I'll crush his ribs like a rotten hazelnut before I cross that threshold! If I don't knock him down now, I'll murder him some day. So if you value his life, let me get at him!”

“He isn't coming,” I interrupted, inventing a small lie. “It's the coachman and both gardeners. Surely you won't wait for them to throw you into the road! They've each got a club, and the master will probably watch from the parlour windows to make sure they obey.”

The coachman and gardeners _were_ there, but Linton was with them. They had already entered the yard. On reflection, Heathcliff decided to avoid fighting three servants. He seized the poker, smashed the lock off the inner door and escaped as they came stamping in.
Mrs. Linton, in great agitation, told me to come upstairs with her. She did not know how much I had contributed to the disturbance, and I wanted to keep her ignorant.

“I'm almost out of my mind, Nelly!” she exclaimed, throwing herself onto the sofa. “A thousand blacksmiths' hammers are pounding in my head! Tell Isabella to keep away. All this is her fault, and if she or anyone else provokes me now, I'll go wild. And Nelly, if you see Edgar again tonight, tell him I'm in danger of serious illness. I hope it proves true. He's shocked and distressed me dreadfully! I want to frighten him. Besides, he might come here and begin abusing me or complaining. I'm sure I'd accuse him in return, and God knows where we'd finish! Will you tell him, my good Nelly? You know I'm not to blame for any of this. What possessed him to listen? Heathcliff spoke outrageously after you left, but I could soon have turned him away from Isabella, and the rest meant nothing. Now everything's ruined by that foolish craving some people have, like a demon haunting them, to hear themselves spoken ill of! If Edgar had never overheard, the conversation would have done him no harm. Really, when he started on me in that unreasonably angry tone, after I'd scolded Heathcliff hoarse for _his_ sake, I scarcely cared what they did to each other. Especially since I felt that, whatever happened, we'd all be driven apart for who knows how long! Well, if I can't keep Heathcliff as my friend, if Edgar insists on being mean and jealous, I'll try to break their hearts by breaking mine. When they drive me to extremes, that would end everything quickly! But it's a last desperate measure; I wouldn't spring it on Linton without warning. Until now he's sensibly feared provoking me. You must explain the danger of changing that policy and remind him how close my passionate temper comes to frenzy once it's roused. I wish you'd get rid of that indifferent look and show a little more concern for me.”

My unmoved reception of these instructions was doubtless infuriating, for she spoke in complete sincerity. But I thought that someone able to plan beforehand how to profit from fits of passion could, by using her will, control herself fairly well even while they lasted. I had no wish to “frighten” her husband, as she put it, and increase his troubles to serve her selfish purposes. So when I met the master heading towards the parlour, I said nothing. I did take the liberty of turning back to hear whether they would quarrel again. He spoke first.

“Stay where you are, Catherine,” he said, without anger but in a deeply sorrowful, dejected voice. “I won't stay. I've come neither to argue nor to make peace. I only want to know whether, after tonight, you mean to continue your close friendship with—”

“Oh, for pity's sake,” the mistress interrupted, stamping her foot, “for pity's sake, say no more about it now! Your cold blood can never rise to a fever; your veins are full of icy water, but mine are boiling, and seeing your coldness makes them leap.”

“Answer my question and I'll go,” Mr. Linton persisted. “You _must_ answer, and this violence doesn't frighten me. I've discovered you can be as self-controlled as anyone when you choose. Will you give up Heathcliff, or give up me? You can't be _my_ friend and _his_ together, and I absolutely _insist_ on knowing which you choose.”
“I insist on being left alone!” Catherine exclaimed furiously. “I demand it! Can't you see I can barely stand? Edgar, you—you must leave me!”

She rang the bell until it broke with a twang; I came in slowly. Such senseless, wicked rages would try a saint's patience! She lay banging her head against the sofa's arm and grinding her teeth as though she meant to shatter them! Mr. Linton stood watching, suddenly full of remorse and fear, and told me to bring water. She had no breath to speak. I fetched a full glass, and when she refused to drink I sprinkled her face. Within seconds she stretched out rigidly and rolled her eyes upward; her cheeks, at once pale and discoloured, took on the appearance of death. Linton looked terrified.
“There's absolutely nothing wrong with her,” I whispered. I didn't want him to give in, though inwardly I could not help feeling afraid.
“Her lips are bloody!” he said with a shudder.

“Never mind!” I answered sharply, and told him that before he came she had planned to display a fit of madness. Carelessly I said this aloud, and she heard. She sprang up, hair flying over her shoulders, eyes flashing, the muscles of her neck and arms standing out unnaturally. I expected broken bones at the very least. Instead she glared round for an instant and rushed away. The master told me to follow, and I did, as far as her bedroom door, which she locked against me.

When she made no move to come down for breakfast next morning, I went to ask if she wanted it brought up. “No!” she replied firmly. I asked again at dinner and tea, and again the following day, always receiving the same answer. Mr. Linton spent his time in the library without asking what his wife was doing. He and Isabella had talked for an hour while he tried to draw from her a properly horrified response to Heathcliff's advances. Her evasive answers told him nothing, and he had to end the questioning unsatisfied. He did, however, solemnly warn her that if she were mad enough to encourage that worthless suitor, every family tie between them would be broken.
